steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using large language models as a natural-language interface between clinicians and AI models / digital health tools. Cover why digital health and clinical AI tools struggle to get adopted, what LLMs could offer and where they fall short, our tool-augmented approach, and the cardiovascular risk-scoring case study we use to demonstrate it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Digital health tools: promise vs. poor clinical adoption; usability; AI adds trust issues
2. Earlier attempts to make clinical predictive models easier to use
3. LLMs as an opportunity in healthcare, and their limitations in clinical settings
4. Our idea: LLMs as an interface to AI models and digital tools
5. Why adaptable dialogue matters; augmenting LLMs with external tools
6. Case study: CVD risk scoring, improved score with AutoPrognosis 2.0, LLM interface

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Digital health tools and adoption
- digital healthcare technologies = frontier in medicine; many tools developed
- clinical adoption faces significant hurdles; some call use "infeasible", "substantially conceptual"
- key issue: usability -> errors associated with patient harm, clinician frustration, jeopardizes patient safety
- AI / machine learning: substantial promise, impact expected across all areas of healthcare
- but same usability challenges + questions around model trust
- => limited uptake and impact of AI in clinical settings so far

2. Making predictive models usable
- simplify/automate obtaining a prediction: points-based scoring systems, web-based calculators, integration in electronic health records
- easier to use, but a prediction alone often insufficient; need to build trust with clinicians and regulators

3. LLMs: opportunity and limits
- potential solution to challenges of digital tools
- captured imagination of research community and general public; pushing boundaries of human-machine interaction
- applications in healthcare: clinical documentation, summarizing research papers, chatbot for patients
- safety-critical settings: inconsistent/nonsensical answers, hallucinated facts -> unacceptable for high-stakes decisions
- trouble with basic functionality (mathematical calculations, factual lookup); no up-to-date information by default
- => limited clinical utility

4. Our proposal
- new application: LLMs to facilitate clinician interactions with AI models and digital tools
- differs from medicine-specific LLMs or LLMs for prediction
- LLM-based systems, intuitive natural language interface, multiple digital tools + information sources -> efficiency, usability (Fig. 1)

5. Dialogue and tool access
- dynamic natural language dialogues identified as key feature for practitioners deploying ML in healthcare
- best interface/dialogue can't be pre-specified; depends on clinician and patient -> adapting/tailoring unlocked by LLMs
- LLMs can't access external tools/information by default -> we augment them with approved medical tools and information sources
- scalable to multiple predictive models; single natural language interface
- systems approach: LLM doesn't issue predictions itself, accesses domain-specific information -> limits hallucinations; actionable info from approved clinical sources

6. Case study: CVD
- risk scoring; cardiovascular disease (CVD) = most common cause of mortality globally
- primary prevention: prognostic models estimate future CVD risk -> identify high-risk individuals, manage risk (lifestyle modifications, pharmaceuticals)
- existing scores: Framingham (United States), SCORE2 (Europe), QRisk3 (UK)
- develop improved CVD risk score with AutoPrognosis 2.0 (open-source automated ML framework for diagnostic/prognostic models)
- novel LLM-based interface for our model + existing scores; illustrative examples of dynamic interactions beyond fixed interfaces

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Digital health technologies are a new frontier in medicine. There are lots of tools being developed, but getting them adopted in the clinic has significant hurdles, and some people have even called their use “infeasible” and “substantially conceptual”. One of the main issues is usability. Poor usability can lead to errors that are associated with patient harm and it adds to clinician frustration, which puts patient safety at risk. New tools that use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are very promising, and their impact is expected to be felt across all areas of healthcare. But these approaches have the same usability problems as the existing digital tools, and on top of that they raise questions about model trust. Because of this, these issues have so far limited how much AI technologies are taken up in clinical settings and how much impact they have there.

Several approaches have tried to make clinical predictive models more usable by simplifying or automating how a prediction is obtained. Examples are points-based scoring systems, web-based calculators, or integrating them into electronic health records. This can make the tools easier to use, but just getting a prediction is often not enough, and more is needed to build model trust with clinicians and also with regulators.

Large Language Models (LLMs) could be a potential solution to the challenges that digital tools face. LLMs have recently captured the imagination of the research community and also the general public, and they are pushing the boundaries of how humans and machines interact. So there is a lot of interest in using LLMs in healthcare, and potential applications include helping with clinical documentation, summarizing research papers, or acting as a chatbot for patients.

But applying LLMs in clinical settings, which are safety-critical, is not straightforward. LLMs can give inconsistent or nonsensical answers and they tend to hallucinate facts. In medicine, where high-stakes decisions are made, this is clearly not acceptable. LLMs can also have difficulty with things that seem basic, like mathematical calculations or looking up facts, and by default they cannot access up-to-date information. All of these limitations constrain how useful LLMs are clinically.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Digital health technologies are a new frontier in medicine. There are lots of tools being developed, but getting them adopted in the clinic has significant hurdles, and some people have even called their use “infeasible” and “substantially conceptual”. One of the main issues is usability. Poor usability can lead to errors that are associated with patient harm and it adds to clinician frustration, which puts patient safety at risk. New tools that use artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning are very promising, and their impact is expected to be felt across all areas of healthcare. But these approaches have the same usability problems as the existing digital tools, and on top of that they raise questions about model trust. Because of this, these issues have so far limited how much AI technologies are taken up in clinical settings and how much impact they have there.

Several approaches have tried to make clinical predictive models more usable by simplifying or automating how a prediction is obtained. Examples are points-based scoring systems, web-based calculators, or integrating them into electronic health records. This can make the tools easier to use, but just getting a prediction is often not enough, and more is needed to build model trust with clinicians and also with regulators.

Large Language Models (LLMs) could be a potential solution to the challenges that digital tools face. LLMs have recently captured the imagination of the research community and also the general public, and they are pushing the boundaries of how humans and machines interact. So there is a lot of interest in using LLMs in healthcare, and potential applications include helping with clinical documentation, summarizing research papers, or acting as a chatbot for patients.

But applying LLMs in clinical settings, which are safety-critical, is not straightforward. LLMs can give inconsistent or nonsensical answers and they tend to hallucinate facts. In medicine, where high-stakes decisions are made, this is clearly not acceptable. LLMs can also have difficulty with things that seem basic, like mathematical calculations or looking up facts, and by default they cannot access up-to-date information. All of these limitations constrain how useful LLMs are clinically.

In this paper we explore a new application of LLMs in healthcare. We propose using LLMs to make it easier for clinicians to interact with AI models and digital tools. This is conceptually quite different from previous applications, for example training LLMs specific to medicine or using LLMs to make predictions. Instead, we build LLM-based systems that offer an intuitive natural language interface, which can streamline how clinicians interact with multiple digital tools and sources of information and improve efficiency and usability (Fig. 1).

Dynamic interactions in the form of natural language dialogues have been identified as a key feature for practitioners to deploy machine learning models in healthcare. The best interface or dialogue can't be specified in advance, because it depends on the clinician and on the patient. So being able to adapt and tailor the interactions is a critical advance in what these tools can do, and LLMs can unlock this.

LLMs by default can't access external tools or information. We augment the basic functionality of LLMs so that they can access approved medical tools and other sources of information, so we are not only relying on the inherent capabilities of whatever LLM is used. The approach scales to multiple predictive models and unifies digital tools in a single interface based on natural language. Because we take a systems approach, the LLM does not issue predictions itself, and it can access relevant domain-specific information instead of having to supply specific knowledge itself. This means the potential for hallucinations is limited and we make sure that actionable information comes from approved clinical sources.

As an example of the approach, we focused specifically on risk scoring and looked at cardiovascular disease (CVD), which is the most common cause of mortality globally. In primary prevention, prognostic models are used to estimate the future risk of developing CVD. This lets high-risk individuals be identified and their risk be managed with interventions, such as lifestyle modifications or pharmaceuticals. Many CVD risk scores have been developed before, for example the Framingham score in the United States, SCORE2 in Europe, and QRisk3 in the UK. First we develop an improved CVD risk score using AutoPrognosis 2.0, which is an open-source automated machine learning framework for developing diagnostic and prognostic models. Then we demonstrate a novel LLM-based interface for our prognostic model and also for existing risk scores. We give several illustrative examples of dynamic interactions that go well beyond what existing fixed interfaces can do.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Digital healthcare technologies represent a frontier in medicine. Although a multitude of tools have been developed [1,2], their clinical adoption faces significant hurdles [3,4], with some even calling their use “infeasible” [5] and “substantially conceptual” [6]. A key issue is usability [7], which can result in errors associated with patient harm [8] and contribute to clinician frustration, jeopardizing patient safety [9,10]. New tools employing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning offer substantial promise, and their impact is expected to be felt across all areas of healthcare [11]. Yet these approaches face the same usability challenges as existing digital tools, while also raising questions around model trust [12,13]. Consequently, these issues have so far limited the uptake and impact of AI technologies in clinical settings [14,15,16].

To improve the usability of clinical predictive models, several approaches have tried to simplify or automate the process of obtaining a prediction. These include points-based scoring systems [17], web-based calculators [18,19], and integration within electronic health records [20]. While this can make such tools easier to use, simply obtaining a prediction is often insufficient, and more is required to build model trust with both clinicians [12] and regulators [21,22].

Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a potential solution to the challenges faced by digital tools. LLMs have recently captured the imagination of both the research community and the general public, pushing the boundaries of human-machine interaction. As a result, there is great interest in applying LLMs in healthcare, with potential applications including facilitating clinical documentation, summarizing research papers, or acting as a chatbot for patients [23].

However, applying LLMs in safety-critical clinical settings is not straightforward. LLMs may provide inconsistent or nonsensical answers [24,25] and tend to hallucinate facts [26,27], which is clearly unacceptable in medicine when making high-stakes decisions. LLMs can also have difficulty with seemingly basic functionality, such as mathematical calculations or factual lookup [28,29], and cannot access up-to-date information by default [30]. These limitations constrain the clinical utility of LLMs.

In this paper, we explore a new application of LLMs in healthcare and propose using LLMs to facilitate clinician interactions with AI models and digital tools. Conceptually, this differs substantially from previous applications, such as training medicine-specific LLMs [31,32] or using LLMs for prediction [33]. Instead, we construct LLM-based systems that offer an intuitive natural language interface, streamlining clinician interactions with multiple digital tools and sources of information and improving efficiency and usability (Fig. 1).

Dynamic interactions in the form of natural language dialogues have been identified as a key feature for practitioners to deploy machine learning models in healthcare [34]. The most appropriate interface or dialogue cannot be specified in advance; it depends on the clinician and the patient. The ability to adapt and tailor interactions therefore represents a critical advance in the functionality of such tools, one that can be unlocked by LLMs.

By default, LLMs cannot access external tools or information. We augment the base functionality of LLMs, enabling them to access approved medical tools and other sources of information, so that we do not rely solely on the inherent capabilities of a given LLM. This approach scales to multiple predictive models, unifying digital tools within a single natural language-based interface. By adopting a systems approach, the LLM does not issue predictions itself and can access relevant domain-specific information instead of needing to supply specific knowledge itself. As a result, the potential for hallucinations is limited, and we ensure that actionable information is provided by approved clinical sources.

As an example of our approach, we focused on risk scoring [35] and considered cardiovascular disease (CVD), the most common cause of mortality globally [36]. Primary prevention uses prognostic models to estimate the future risk of developing CVD, allowing high-risk individuals to be identified and their risk to be managed via interventions such as lifestyle modifications or pharmaceuticals. Numerous CVD risk scores have been developed previously, for example the Framingham score [37] in the United States, SCORE2 [38] in Europe, and QRisk3 [18] in the UK. We begin by developing an improved risk score for CVD using AutoPrognosis 2.0 [19], an open-source automated machine learning framework for developing diagnostic and prognostic models. We then demonstrate a novel LLM-based interface for both our prognostic model and existing risk scores, and provide several illustrative examples of dynamic interactions that substantially extend what existing fixed interfaces can do.
